sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Containers package applications and their required components so workloads can run consistently across environments.
This objective is not asking you to become a container engineer.

You need to recognize a container running by itself, multiple containers being managed together, how container ports are exposed, what happens to container data, and where container images are stored.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Is the scenario about running, coordinating, connecting, storing data for, or obtaining containers?
sections.callout: Container lifecycle clue → identify the matching container concept.

sections.title: Stand-Alone
paragraphs: A stand-alone container operates independently without requiring a larger orchestration platform to coordinate a group of containers.
This can work well for simple workloads.
Think: One container, one job.
sections.callout: If a container simply needs to run by itself without fleet management → think stand-alone.

sections.title: Workload Orchestration
paragraphs: As container environments grow, manually managing every container becomes difficult.
Workload orchestration coordinates containers and their workloads.
An orchestration platform can help manage placement, deployment, scaling, recovery, and coordination.
Think: The conductor managing the container orchestra.
sections.callout: If many containers must be automatically coordinated → think workload orchestration.

sections.title: Networking
paragraphs: Containers can run services that listen on network ports.
Container networking governs how containers communicate with hosts, other containers, and external services.

entries.title: Port Mapping
paragraphs: Port mapping connects a port exposed outside the container to the appropriate port used by the application inside the container.
Think: Outside door → container door.
An application may listen on a particular port inside its container while external clients reach it through a mapped host port.
entries.recognitionCue: If users need to reach an application running on a container's internal port → think port mapping.

sections.title: Storage Types
paragraphs: Container storage can either persist beyond a container's life or remain temporary with that workload.

entries.title: Persistent Volumes
paragraphs: Containers are often designed to be replaceable. That becomes a problem when the application needs data to survive after the container disappears.
A persistent volume stores data separately so that data remains available beyond the life of one container.
Think: Container dies; data survives.
Examples include application data that must remain after a container restart or replacement.
entries.recognitionCue: If data must survive container deletion or recreation → think persistent volume.

entries.title: Ephemeral Storage
paragraphs: Ephemeral storage exists only temporarily with the workload.
When the container is removed, the data may disappear with it.
Think: Temporary container, temporary data.
It works well for temporary files or information that does not need long-term retention.
entries.recognitionCue: If the data can disappear when the container disappears → think ephemeral storage.

sections.title: Image Registries
paragraphs: Before a container can run, its image must come from somewhere.
An image registry stores and distributes container images.
A system can retrieve the required image and use it to launch containers.
Think: Container image warehouse.
sections.callout: If the scenario asks where container images are stored or retrieved → think image registry.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Many containers need coordination → Workload orchestration
Connect external port to container service → Port mapping
Data must survive container replacement → Persistent volume
Store or distribute container images → Image registry

entries.title: Image vs. Container
paragraphs: The image is the stored template used to create the workload. The container is the running instance created from that image.
The objective specifically lists image registries, meaning the place used to keep container images.

entries.title: Persistent vs. Ephemeral
paragraphs: Do not select based simply on whether the application uses storage.
Ask whether the data must survive after the container is destroyed. Yes points to persistent; no points to ephemeral.

entries.title: Stand-Alone vs. Orchestration
paragraphs: One or a few simple containers may run stand-alone. Large groups requiring automated coordination point toward orchestration.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Container-to-host, container-to-container, or external communication → Networking
External port needs to reach container application → Port mapping
Container disappears but data must remain → Persistent volume
Need a repository for container images → Image registry
